notes:
1. Utility of a Government Scheme — Meaning

  • The utility of a government scheme means the extent to which it actually solves the problem for which it was created.
  • Announcement, budget allocation or application numbers alone do not prove usefulness.
📌 Must-Memorise

Scheme Utility → Intended Problem Actually Reduced

2. Central Evaluation Question

The most important question is:

Did the Scheme Produce the Intended Benefit?

  • Utility must ultimately be established through beneficiary outcomes.

3. Expenditure vs Utility

  • A programme may spend its entire allocation and still fail to produce the intended improvement.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Scheme Expenditure ≠ Scheme Utility

4. Why Evaluation Is Necessary

Evaluation helps determine:

  • Whether objectives are being achieved.
  • Who receives benefits.
  • Which implementation problems exist.
  • Whether redesign or expansion is needed.
  • Whether schemes should be integrated.

5. Limited Public Resources

  • Government money, staff and administrative capacity are limited.
  • Evaluation helps decide how these resources should be allocated among competing needs.
📌 Must-Memorise

Evaluation → Better Use of Scarce Public Resources

6. Purpose of Evaluation

Evaluation should support:

  • Learning.
  • Accountability.
  • Policy improvement.
  • Course correction.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Evaluation ≠ Merely Finding Faults

7. Evaluation Cycle

The basic programme-evaluation cycle is:

Scheme

→ Implementation

→ Measurement

→ Evaluation

→ Improvement

📌 Must-Memorise

Evaluation Should Lead to Course Correction

8. Input–Output–Outcome–Impact Framework

A major scheme-assessment distinction is between:

  • Input.
  • Output.
  • Outcome.
  • Impact.

9. Input

Inputs are resources used by the programme.

Examples:

  • Money.
  • Staff.
  • Buildings.
  • Equipment.
📌 Must-Memorise

Money/Staff/Infrastructure → Input

10. Output

Output means the immediate goods or services produced.

Example:

  • Number of meals served.
  • Number of beneficiaries paid.
  • Number of houses constructed.
📌 Must-Memorise

Service Delivered → Output

11. Outcome

Outcome means the change experienced by beneficiaries.

Examples:

  • Better attendance.
  • Lower dropout.
  • Improved nutrition.
  • Better access to treatment.
📌 Must-Memorise

Beneficiary Condition Improved → Outcome

12. Impact

Impact refers to broader, often longer-term developmental change.

Examples:

  • Higher educational attainment.
  • Improved employability.
  • Reduced intergenerational deprivation.

13. Input–Output–Outcome–Impact Chain

The distinction can be remembered as:

Money Spent → Input

Service Delivered → Output

Beneficiary Improves → Outcome

Long-Term Change → Impact

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Output ≠ Outcome

14. Output-Outcome Monitoring

  • The supplied source notes that government monitoring has increasingly shifted from merely tracking inputs towards measurable outputs and outcomes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Modern Monitoring → From Spending to Results

15. Coverage — Meaning

Coverage measures how much of the intended population is actually reached by a scheme.

16. Coverage Rate

A simplified formula is:

Coverage Rate = Beneficiaries Reached ÷ Eligible Population × 100

📌 Must-Memorise

Coverage → Reach of Intended Population

17. Why Coverage Matters

Coverage is important particularly for programmes involving:

  • Food security.
  • Vaccination.
  • School education.
  • Social protection.

18. Coverage Limitation

  • A programme may have very high coverage but still provide a weak or inadequate benefit.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

High Coverage ≠ High Impact

19. Targeting

Targeted programmes select beneficiaries using criteria such as:

  • Income.
  • Age.
  • Gender.
  • Disability.
  • Occupation.
  • Education.
  • Social category.

20. Exclusion Error

An exclusion error occurs when:

An Eligible Person Does Not Receive the Benefit

📌 Must-Memorise

Exclusion Error → Deserving Beneficiary Left Out

21. Inclusion Error

An inclusion error occurs when:

An Ineligible Person Receives the Benefit

📌 Must-Memorise

Inclusion Error → Wrong Beneficiary Included

22. Ideal Targeting

A good targeting system should:

  • Minimise exclusion errors.
  • Minimise inclusion errors.
  • Avoid unnecessary documentation barriers.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Better Targeting ≠ Maximum Documentation

23. Accessibility

A scheme may exist but remain difficult to use because of:

  • Distance.
  • Complicated procedures.
  • Documentation.
  • Digital literacy.
  • Lack of awareness.
  • Disability barriers.

24. Availability vs Accessibility

  • A benefit can be administratively available but practically inaccessible.
📌 Must-Memorise

Availability + Accessibility → Practical Access

25. Digital Access — Dual Effect

Digital applications can:

  • Improve convenience for some citizens.
  • Create barriers for those lacking devices, connectivity or digital skills.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Digitalisation ≠ Automatic Accessibility

26. Simplified Procedures

Useful welfare administration should reduce:

  • Repeated office visits.
  • Unnecessary certificates.
  • Excessive application stages.
📌 Must-Memorise

Simple Procedure → Greater Access → Greater Utility

27. Benefit Adequacy

Benefit adequacy asks whether the amount, quantity or service provided is sufficient to address the intended problem.

28. Adequacy and Inflation

  • A monetary benefit may lose real value if prices rise while the benefit remains unchanged for many years.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nominal Benefit Can Fall in Real Value

29. Adequacy Test

The correct question is:

Is the Benefit Sufficient to Produce the Intended Outcome?

  • Higher expenditure by itself does not prove adequacy.

30. Timeliness

Some schemes are useful only when delivered at the correct time.

Examples:

  • Scholarship during the academic period.
  • Farm support during cultivation season.
  • Emergency care immediately.
  • Pension regularly.

31. Delayed Benefits

  • A correct benefit delivered too late may lose much of its usefulness.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Correct Benefit Delivered Late ≠ Fully Effective Benefit

32. Continuity

Some programmes require uninterrupted support.

Examples include:

  • Chronic-disease treatment.
  • Social pensions.
  • Educational assistance.
📌 Must-Memorise

Utility Depends on Amount + Timing + Regularity

33. Equity — Meaning

Equity analysis asks:

Who Benefits Most?

Important dimensions include:

  • Income.
  • Gender.
  • Caste.
  • Disability.
  • Region.
  • Rural–urban location.

34. Distributional Utility

A scheme has stronger distributional utility when it improves access for groups facing greater disadvantage.

📌 Must-Memorise

Average Benefit Alone Is Not Enough

35. Vidiyal Payanam — Evaluation Example

  • The supplied source notes that Tamil Nadu State Planning Commission evaluation of Vidiyal Payanam examined beneficiary characteristics and found especially strong benefits among lower-income women.

36. Multiple Utility

A single scheme can create several benefits.

For example, a mobility scheme may generate:

  • Transport savings.
  • Better work access.
  • Educational access.
  • Greater independence.
📌 Must-Memorise

One Scheme → Multiple Forms of Utility

37. Cost-Effectiveness

Cost-effectiveness compares:

Programme Cost ↔ Outcome Achieved

  • It asks whether meaningful outcomes are being produced efficiently.

38. Cost-Effectiveness vs Cheapest Programme

  • The cheapest programme is not automatically the most cost-effective.
  • Some important social benefits are difficult to value purely in rupees.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Cost-Effective ≠ Cheapest

39. Opportunity Cost

  • Money spent on one programme cannot simultaneously be spent elsewhere.
  • This makes scheme prioritisation important.
📌 Must-Memorise

Public Expenditure Has Opportunity Cost

40. Utility of Food-Security Schemes

Food-security schemes can be evaluated through:

  • Availability of commodities.
  • Access.
  • Household food security.
  • Protection against price shocks.

41. Utility of School Nutrition

For a school-meal programme:

  • Meals served → Output.
  • Better attendance/nutrition → Outcome.
  • Better educational development → Longer-term impact.
📌 Must-Memorise

Meals Served ≠ Final Measure of Success

42. Utility of Educational Welfare

Education-support schemes should be evaluated through:

  • Enrolment.
  • Retention.
  • Dropout reduction.
  • Course completion.
  • Employment transition.

43. Pudhumai Penn — Evaluation Logic

The supplied source uses the following logic:

  • Money transferred → Output.
  • Student continues higher education → Outcome.
  • Better employment/social mobility → Potential impact.
📌 Must-Memorise

Educational Utility → Retention + Qualification + Capability

44. Utility of Health Schemes

Health schemes can produce:

  • Health utility.
  • Financial utility.

Important evaluation questions include:

  • Was treatment obtained?
  • Was it geographically accessible?
  • Did financial hardship fall?
  • Was catastrophic expenditure reduced?

45. CMCHIS — Utility Logic

CMCHIS should be evaluated through:

Health Risk

→ Treatment Access

→ Financial Protection

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Number of Claims Paid ≠ Complete Measure of Health Utility

46. Utility of Social Pensions

Social pensions can be useful when they help vulnerable beneficiaries maintain:

  • Food consumption.
  • Medicines.
  • Basic expenses.
  • Minimum economic security.
📌 Must-Memorise

Social Pension Utility → Consumption Stability

47. Productive Utility of Welfare

Welfare can produce productive benefits through:

  • Better nutrition.
  • Better health.
  • Higher education.
  • Improved skills.

48. Human-Capital Utility

Examples include:

Better Nutrition → Better Learning

Education Support → Higher Skills

Health Care → Greater Work Capacity

📌 Must-Memorise

Welfare Utility Can Extend Beyond Immediate Consumption

49. Universal Schemes

Universal schemes provide broad coverage.

Potential advantages:

  • Lower exclusion risk.
  • Simpler eligibility.
  • Wider social acceptance.

Tamil Nadu's Universal PDS is an example cited in the source.

50. Targeted Schemes

Targeted schemes concentrate benefits on specified groups.

Potential advantage:

  • More focused use of resources.

Potential weakness:

  • Identification and exclusion problems.

51. Universal vs Targeted — Utility

There is no universal rule that one is always superior.

The choice depends on:

  • Nature of problem.
  • Fiscal capacity.
  • Administrative capacity.
  • Exclusion risk.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Universal vs Targeted ≠ Good vs Bad

52. Beneficiary Satisfaction

Beneficiary feedback can reveal:

  • Ease of access.
  • Hidden costs.
  • Service quality.
  • Practical usefulness.

53. Satisfaction vs Objective Outcomes

  • Satisfaction is useful but should not be the only measure.
  • A beneficiary may like a programme even when the intended long-term outcome is weak.
📌 Must-Memorise

Best Evaluation → Beneficiary Feedback + Objective Outcome Data

54. Monitoring

Monitoring is a continuous process asking:

  • Is implementation progressing?
  • Are targets being met?
  • Are services being delivered?
📌 Must-Memorise

Monitoring → Is It Being Implemented?

55. Evaluation

Evaluation asks:

  • Did the programme actually work?
  • What changed?
  • Why did it work or fail?
  • For whom did it work best?
📌 Must-Memorise

Evaluation → Is It Actually Working?

56. Monitoring vs Evaluation

  • Monitoring → Continuous implementation tracking.
  • Evaluation → Deeper assessment of effectiveness and impact.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Monitoring ≠ Evaluation

57. Tamil Nadu State Planning Commission — Role

  • The supplied source notes that the Tamil Nadu State Planning Commission evaluates flagship programmes to assess outcomes and improve policy.
  • Examples cited include:
  • Pudhumai Penn.
  • Breakfast Scheme.
  • Vidiyal Payanam.
  • Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam.
  • Illam Thedi Kalvi.

58. Evidence-Based Scheme Decisions

Evaluation may lead to:

  • Continue.
  • Expand.
  • Modify.
  • Converge.
  • Rationalise.
  • Replace or discontinue.
📌 Must-Memorise

Scheme Continuation Should Follow Evidence, Not Inertia

59. TNPSC Traps

  • Scheme announcement does not prove scheme utility.
  • Budget allocation does not prove success.
  • Applications received do not prove outcome.
  • Scheme expenditure and scheme utility are different.
  • Evaluation is intended for learning and improvement, not merely fault-finding.
  • Input means resources used.
  • Output means immediate service or good delivered.
  • Outcome means change in beneficiary condition.
  • Impact means broader long-term development change.
  • Money spent → Input.
  • Meals served → Output.
  • Better attendance → Outcome.
  • Higher educational attainment → Impact.
  • Output and outcome should never be used interchangeably.
  • High expenditure does not necessarily mean high output.
  • High output does not necessarily mean high outcome.
  • Coverage measures reach, not quality.
  • Coverage rate uses beneficiaries reached relative to eligible population.
  • High coverage does not guarantee high impact.
  • Exclusion error → eligible person left out.
  • Inclusion error → ineligible person receives benefit.
  • Maximum documentation does not necessarily improve targeting.
  • Complex verification can itself create exclusion.
  • Scheme availability and scheme accessibility are different.
  • Digital-only applications can create exclusion.
  • Simplification can increase scheme utility.
  • Benefit adequacy must be judged relative to actual need.
  • Inflation can reduce the real value of monetary benefits.
  • Larger monetary benefit does not automatically mean better scheme design.
  • Timeliness is especially important for scholarships, farm assistance and emergency health care.
  • Delayed welfare can lose much of its usefulness.
  • Continuity matters for pensions and chronic-disease treatment.
  • Equity asks who benefits, not merely how many benefit.
  • Average benefit can hide unequal distribution.
  • Vidiyal Payanam illustrates multiple utility.
  • A transport scheme may produce mobility, employment and empowerment benefits simultaneously.
  • Cost-effectiveness is not the same as choosing the cheapest programme.
  • Public spending has opportunity cost.
  • Social benefits such as dignity may be difficult to monetise.
  • Food distributed is an output; improved food security is an outcome.
  • Meals served are not the final measure of school-nutrition success.
  • Education welfare should ultimately be linked with retention and completion.
  • Money transferred under educational support is an output, not necessarily the final outcome.
  • Health claims processed do not by themselves prove better health.
  • Health utility includes both access and financial protection.
  • Social pensions should be assessed by economic security, not only payment count.
  • Welfare can create productive human-capital benefits.
  • Universal schemes may reduce exclusion risk.
  • Targeted schemes may concentrate resources.
  • Neither universal nor targeted welfare is automatically superior in every situation.
  • Beneficiary satisfaction and actual outcomes are different.
  • Monitoring is continuous implementation tracking.
  • Evaluation examines effectiveness and causation more deeply.
  • Monitoring and evaluation should complement each other.
  • Tamil Nadu State Planning Commission conducts evaluation of flagship schemes.
  • Evaluation may justify expansion of a successful scheme.
  • Evaluation may also justify modification, convergence or rationalisation.
  • A scheme should not continue unchanged merely because it has existed for many years.
  • Evidence-based governance requires course correction.
  • Final utility principle → Objective + Reach + Access + Adequacy + Timeliness + Equity + Outcome.

60. Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected

  • Scheme utility means? → Extent to which the intended problem is actually solved.
  • Scheme expenditure equals utility? → No.
  • Main evaluation question? → Did the scheme produce the intended benefit?
  • Why evaluate schemes? → Learning, accountability and policy improvement.
  • Evaluation cycle? → Scheme → Implementation → Measurement → Evaluation → Improvement.
  • Four programme-performance levels? → Input, output, outcome and impact.
  • Input means? → Resources used.
  • Output means? → Immediate goods/services delivered.
  • Outcome means? → Change in beneficiary condition.
  • Impact means? → Broader long-term developmental change.
  • Money spent? → Input.
  • Meals served? → Output.
  • Better attendance? → Outcome.
  • Higher educational attainment? → Impact.
  • Coverage means? → Extent to which eligible population is reached.
  • Coverage formula? → Beneficiaries reached ÷ eligible population × 100.
  • High coverage guarantees impact? → No.
  • Exclusion error? → Eligible beneficiary left out.
  • Inclusion error? → Ineligible beneficiary included.
  • Better targeting means maximum paperwork? → No.
  • Accessibility means? → Ease with which intended beneficiaries can obtain the benefit.
  • Digitalisation always increases access? → No.
  • Benefit adequacy means? → Whether assistance is sufficient to address the need.
  • Inflation can affect welfare how? → Reduce real value of fixed monetary benefits.
  • Timeliness means? → Benefit reaches beneficiary when it is actually needed.
  • Correct but delayed benefit fully effective? → No.
  • Continuity important for? → Pensions, chronic care and educational support.
  • Equity analysis asks? → Who benefits?
  • Average benefit alone sufficient? → No.
  • Vidiyal Payanam illustrates? → Multiple utility.
  • Cost-effectiveness means? → Efficient use of resources to achieve meaningful outcomes.
  • Cost-effective always means cheapest? → No.
  • Opportunity cost means? → Resources used for one purpose cannot simultaneously be used elsewhere.
  • Food delivered is? → Output.
  • Better food security is? → Outcome.
  • Educational scheme success measured only by money transferred? → No.
  • Pudhumai Penn utility ultimately linked to? → Higher-education retention and longer-term mobility.
  • CMCHIS utility should include? → Treatment access + financial protection.
  • Social pension utility? → Minimum consumption and income stability.
  • Human-capital welfare includes? → Nutrition, health, education and skills.
  • Universal scheme advantage? → Lower exclusion risk.
  • Targeted scheme advantage? → Concentration of resources.
  • Universal always superior? → No.
  • Targeted always superior? → No.
  • Beneficiary satisfaction enough for evaluation? → No.
  • Best evaluation combines? → Beneficiary feedback + objective data.
  • Monitoring means? → Continuous implementation tracking.
  • Evaluation means? → Assessing whether and why a scheme works.
  • Monitoring and evaluation same? → No.
  • Tamil Nadu institution evaluating flagship schemes? → State Planning Commission.
  • Examples evaluated in source? → Pudhumai Penn, Breakfast Scheme, Vidiyal Payanam, Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam and Illam Thedi Kalvi.
  • Possible post-evaluation decisions? → Continue, expand, modify, converge, rationalise or replace.
  • Scheme continuation should follow? → Evidence.
  • Main outcome-oriented governance principle? → Spend → Measure → Learn → Improve.
  • Complete utility test? → Reach + Access + Adequacy + Timeliness + Equity + Outcome.
  • Core chapter chain? → Scheme Design → Delivery → Beneficiary Outcome → Evaluation → Policy Improvement.
